issues.title: swe-prep: the way to a build-ready spec
issues.body:
## Destination

A build-ready spec for **swe-prep**: a single-user, habit-forming interview-prep app that runs your code, with the exercise/runner seam designed to hold multiple languages and multiple SWE domains.
The map is done when nothing is left to decide before someone opens an editor and builds it.

## Notes

**Domain.** Personal interview-prep tool for an entry-level SWE job hunt, on a few-months horizon.

**Skills every session should consult.** `/grilling` and `/domain-modeling` by default; `/prototype` for the tickets labelled `wayfinder:prototype`; `/research` for `wayfinder:research`.

**The overriding constraint.** The captain is not currently studying consistently.
The tool's real job is to *manufacture* the daily habit, not to organise an existing one.
Every decision on this map should be weighed against one question: does this get him doing a drill every day, sooner?
A feature that delays the first daily session is working against the project's purpose, however good it is.

**Settled while charting (do not relitigate without new information):**

- **Single user, forever.** Built in public so the repo and commit history work as a portfolio artifact, but there is exactly one user and no multi-user tax is paid anywhere.
- **The app runs code.** Because there is no untrusted code (the only author is the only user), execution needs no sandbox or container. This collapses the hardest part of a LeetCode clone into a subprocess or a WASM runtime.
- **Content is a curated fixed set**, starting from Blind 75, expandable to NeetCode 150 later without structural change. Problems are chosen by firstmate; the captain does not approve them individually. Volume is explicitly not the goal - re-solving the right problems on a schedule is.
- **Java is the default solving language**, because it is what the captain would type in a real interview. Languages are pluggable behind a runner adapter, not hardcoded.
- **Sequencing.** Design the exercise abstraction to hold every domain; ship Java algorithms in v1; SQL close behind, because grading it is the same shape as grading code and needs only an embedded engine. Front end is deliberately NOT in v1 - auto-grading it needs a headless browser plus per-exercise DOM assertions, it is the domain where auto-grading is weakest, and it would push the first daily session out by a month or more.

## Decisions so far

<!-- one line per closed ticket: enough to judge relevance, then open the link for the detail -->

- [What one daily session actually looks like](https://github.com/KyleNaluan/swe-prep/issues/3) - Three tiers, only the first required: a ~4-minute, ~8-rep warm-up that alone earns the streak; an optional ~30-minute main exercise; then open-ended continuation. The small core exists because bad days are the only days that matter. The session is domain-agnostic - nothing in it may assume the content is an algorithm problem.

**The session is domain-agnostic (settled by the daily-session ticket).**
Algorithms are not the only purpose of this app.
Warm-up reps and main exercises draw from whatever domains are active.
No part of the session shape may assume algorithm content.
This is a hard requirement on the exercise abstraction rather than a later enhancement.

- [How a submission is judged](https://github.com/KyleNaluan/swe-prep/issues/5) - Pass/fail, no partial credit. On failure the app reports only how many tests failed; the failing case is revealed on request, recorded visibly, never penalised. Claimed complexity is self-reported first, then checked by measuring scaling empirically at growing input sizes. Style feedback none; resource limits reported not graded; every attempt persisted as scheduler input.

- [Where swe-prep runs, and what it is built with](https://github.com/KyleNaluan/swe-prep/issues/2) - A local web app (the only shape that holds front-end grading later), on the captain's existing banking-app stack: Spring Boot 3.4.3 / Java 21, Postgres, React + Vite, Monaco editor, autostarted as a user service. Reached over the tailnet rather than hosted. Hosting later is protected by three cheap decisions taken now, not built.

- [The exercise and runner abstraction](https://github.com/KyleNaluan/swe-prep/issues/6) - `Grader` decides pass/fail, `Runner` only executes, and keeping them apart is what lets concept exercises need no Runner at all. Test cases are **language-neutral JSON data**, with a per-language adapter supplying the harness, so a case is authored once and runs in every language ever added. `Form` (Rep vs Challenge) is an attribute, not a type. LeetCode's tree/list serialisation adopted rather than reinvented.

- [What a warm-up rep is, across domains](https://github.com/KyleNaluan/swe-prep/issues/9) - Five types (pattern ID, complexity, fill-in-the-blank, predict-output, spot-the-bug), multiple choice by default with predict-output free text. Reps train recognition; production is what Challenges are for. **Nearly all reps derive from the problem set** (~5-6 per problem, so ~400 from 75), which collapses the feared second content pile into one. Explanations shown on wrong answers, one keystroke away on correct ones, and asking is recorded as a confidence signal.

- [How the app chooses what you practise next](https://github.com/KyleNaluan/swe-prep/issues/8) - **Two schedulers over one record**: a due-date SRS queue for Reps (cheap, so classic spacing works) and a priority score for Challenges (scarce, so "what is worth 40 minutes today" beats "what is owed"). Attempt records collapse to a 0-5 quality score; time-taken deliberately excluded as noise. Review debt first, weekly cap on new problems, retire rather than delete. Plus an "interview soon" mode that re-weights toward broad recency.

- [What makes a single-player streak actually stick](https://github.com/KyleNaluan/swe-prep/issues/7) - **No invented currency at all.** Solutions commit to a *private* repo with private contributions shown, so the GitHub graph is a true external record without publishing solutions. XP is replaced by an honest readiness picture (patterns covered, shaky topics, solved-cold count) derived from records already kept - which also settles what "ready" means. Plus a scheduled cue, the streak as a record rather than a currency, and a capped repair mechanic so one bad evening does not end the habit.

- [What a SQL exercise actually looks like](https://github.com/KyleNaluan/swe-prep/issues/10) - The same Postgres, a separate fixture database, per-attempt transaction rollback and a read-only role; dialect parity is why it is not an embedded engine. Two or three **shared** schemas with many exercises each, so a schema is learned once rather than re-read every exercise. Multiset row comparison, columns by position, names and row order ignored unless asked; row count is the minimal failure signal and is unusually diagnostic (over-count means join fan-out). ~25-40 exercises. No complexity target.

- [Whether Blind 75 problem statements can ship in a public repo](https://github.com/KyleNaluan/swe-prep/issues/4) - **Public engine, private content.** The private-solutions decision already collapsed this: statements, tests, reference solutions and generators all live in the private content repo (loaded via private submodule or gitignored path), so the public repo holds the engine, the problem *titles* (a free fact) and optionally a few original demo statements - zero protected prose. Scraping is barred by LeetCode's ToS independent of copyright. A permissive wrapper licence does not cure scraped provenance (APPS, CodeContests); only HumanEval, MBPP and Exercism are genuinely clean, and none of them are interview-curated. Full report: `data/swe-license-r4/report.md`.

## Not yet specified

- **Query plans as a SQL topic.** Deferred by the SQL decision, not rejected. A real interview topic but shallow at entry level, and grading on `EXPLAIN` output is a research project. If it ever happens it belongs as a rep type ("which of these uses the index?"), never a graded exercise.
- **Which second language proves the seam, and when.** The abstraction claims a test case authored once runs in any language, but that claim is untested until a second adapter exists. Until then it is a design intention rather than a demonstrated property. Decide which language, and whether it lands in v1 or immediately after.
- **The concepts and flashcard layer.** Wanted, and explicitly a later phase riding the same rails as the coding drills. Cannot be specified until the exercise abstraction exists.
- **Front-end practice.** In scope for the product eventually, but the decision to build it is deferred until the habit is real and the abstraction is proven. Revisit as its own decision with the grading cost understood, not as an assumed feature.
- **The content-entry workflow.** The authoring unit is **statement + test cases + reference solution + input generator**, all of it living in the private content repo, with the warm-up reps derived from it. Licensing is settled, so what remains is purely practical: how the first tranche actually gets entered, and whether any tooling is worth building for it. Still the most likely place this project stalls after the fun engineering is done.
- **LLM code analysis as a complement to empirical complexity measurement.** Deliberately deferred, not rejected - the captain wants this open for later. The two methods fail in completely different ways: measurement is ground truth but coarse and cannot name a complexity or explain it, while an LLM reading the code is precise and explanatory but occasionally confidently wrong, with no reliable signal for when. The design to build if it happens: run both and **surface disagreement rather than picking a winner**, since a disagreement is either a missed subtlety or a case where constant factors lie, and both deserve attention. Known weak spots for the model: amortised analysis, memoised recursion, and hidden library costs (Java string concatenation in a loop, `List.contains()`, `substring()` copying). A confidently wrong verdict in a study tool is worse than no verdict.
- **Large-input generators for complexity measurement.** Required by the judging decision, one per problem, on top of correctness cases. Shape depends on the exercise format; adds to the content-authoring load.
- **Whether reference solutions are shown, and when.** Interacts with how a submission is judged and with the spaced-repetition schedule.

## Out of scope

<!-- ruled beyond the destination; closed, never graduates -->

- **Multi-user support**: accounts, signup, onboarding, hosting for *other learners*. Ruled out by the single-user destination. If this is ever wanted it is a fresh effort, not a resumption of this map.
  **A small shared instance for a few close acquaintances was raised and deliberately left out of scope** (2026-08-04), with the cost understood so it is not rediscovered from scratch. Already paid for by decisions taken for other reasons: authentication (every person-owned row already carries a user id), hosting (Postgres from the start), and per-user progress. **Not** paid for: the execution sandbox, which is the real jump and which "close acquaintances" does not soften - the risk is an accidental infinite loop and the fact that any internet-reachable code-execution service gets probed, so it needs per-submission containers, resource caps, timeouts and network isolation. The `Runner` interface makes that a swap rather than a rewrite, but the container runner is genuine security-sensitive work. Content licensing also gets sharper, since distributing problem statements to other people is a stronger exposure than a private personal copy. One genuine upside if it ever happens: shared use supplies the human accountability that no solo mechanic can replicate.
  **Do not confuse this with single-user hosted access.** The captain deploying swe-prep so *he* can reach it without his PC running is in scope as a protected future goal (see the platform ticket) and is explicitly not this. The distinction is other people, not deployment.

issues.title: Where swe-prep runs, and what it is built with
issues.body:
Part of #1

## Question

Where does swe-prep run, and what is it built with?

A daily-habit app lives or dies on friction at the moment of opening it.
Whatever is chosen has to be openable and into-a-problem in seconds, on whatever machine the captain is actually at when the habit is supposed to fire.

Decide the shape (local web app, desktop app, CLI/TUI, or something else), where state lives, and the stack.
Weigh it primarily against time-to-first-keystroke, and secondarily against being a credible portfolio artifact, since the repo is public and doubles as interview evidence.

Constraints already settled on the map: single user, no auth, no hosting for others, code executes locally with no sandbox required, Java is the default solving language.

Note the interaction with the runner: whatever the shape, it must be able to invoke a JDK and capture results.
issues.author: KyleNaluan

comments.body:
## Resolution: a local Spring Boot web app on the captain's existing stack, designed so hosting later is a deployment project rather than a rewrite

**Shape: a local web app.**
The captain wants front-end practice eventually, and grading that means rendering and asserting in a browser.
A terminal app can never do it and a desktop app would have to embed a browser to fake it, so a web app is the only shape that holds every named domain without a second platform later.
This is decided by domain coverage, not by friction - a TUI would genuinely have had the lowest friction for a heavy terminal user.

**The friction objection is answered by autostart.**
A web app's weakness is "is the server running", and this machine already runs systemd user units for exactly this purpose.
Autostart it, bookmark it, and time-to-first-keystroke is one click with no cold start.

**Stack: reuse [Team-7-Banking-Application](https://github.com/KyleNaluan/Team-7-Banking-Application).**
That repo is already almost exactly this stack, so there is no learning cost and no stack-selection risk:

- **Spring Boot 3.4.3 on Java 21**, with Spring Web, Data JPA, Actuator, Lombok.
- **Postgres**, not SQLite. Already in use, already behind JPA, industry default, a resume keyword, and it removes any database migration if the app is ever hosted. SQLite's only real advantage was needing no service, which is worth little against something already configured.
- **React + Vite** for the front end, as in the banking app.
- **Monaco** for the code editor - what VS Code and LeetCode both use, so it will feel immediately familiar.

Building the backend in Java on Spring Boot is deliberate: entry-level Java postings overwhelmingly screen for Spring Boot, so the codebase itself is portfolio evidence, and the captain writes Java daily while building the tool that trains him in it.

**Reach: tailnet now, hosting protected for later.**

The captain does not need hosted access today.
Tailscale is already working on this machine and already used to reach another local service from a phone, so running locally and reaching it over the tailnet covers the real cases at zero cost, with the one accepted limitation that the PC must be on.

Hosting later is an explicit goal the design must protect, but it is not being built now.
**Note that this is single-user hosted access, which is distinct from the multi-user product ruled out on the map. Do not confuse the two.**

Three cheap decisions buy hosting-later entirely, and cost nothing today:

1. **Postgres from the start** - no migration.
2. **The runner stays behind an interface** - a local-process runner now, a container runner later, swapped rather than rewritten. This is a requirement on the exercise/runner abstraction.
3. **Model the user from day one; skip authentication.** Every row belonging to a person (attempts, streak, schedule state) carries a user id, and exactly one user is seeded. No login screen, no password, no session.

That last one is the important one and is often got backwards.
The expensive part of adding auth later is not Spring Security - the captain has already built that once - it is discovering the schema assumed a single implicit user and threading ownership through every table and query afterwards.
Carrying a user id from the start makes adding auth roughly a day's work; omitting it makes it a refactor that touches everything.

Building the login now would also put a login screen between the captain and his daily drill, which is added friction to the one thing whose entire purpose is removing friction.

**What actually gets expensive when hosted, for whoever picks this up later:** not the database - code execution.
Running locally there is no untrusted code, which is what collapsed the hardest part of a LeetCode clone.
On a server, even single-user, a runaway submission consumes a paid box, so timeouts and resource limits become mandatory; opening it to anyone else brings the full untrusted-code problem (per-submission containers, resource caps, network isolation).
A VM that runs a JVM and spawns JDK processes is realistically $5-20/month.
comments.author: KyleNaluan

comments.body: Record-keeping note: the build diverged from this decision as shipped - spring-boot-starter-jdbc (JdbcClient) instead of Spring Data JPA, no Lombok, and Boot 3.4.7 rather than 3.4.3. Noting it here so the decision record stays honest; the divergence is deliberate-in-practice and documented in the repo overview.

issues.title: What one daily session actually looks like
issues.body:
Part of #1

## Question

What does one daily session actually look like?

This is the unit the whole product is built to deliver, so its shape constrains nearly everything else on the map.

Settle: how long a session is meant to take, how many exercises it contains, what happens when the captain gets one wrong, what happens when he gets stuck, and what "done for today" means.
Also settle whether a session is a fixed daily serving or an open-ended practice surface, and whether partial completion counts.

Build a cheap, rough artifact to react to rather than deciding this in the abstract - an outline, a paper sketch, or a throwaway stub of the session flow.
The honest test to apply: would the captain, on a bad day with low motivation, actually open this and finish it?

Bear in mind the session has to work for a hard algorithm problem that might take 40 minutes, which sits awkwardly with a Duolingo-style short daily serving. Resolving that tension is the substance of this ticket.
issues.author: KyleNaluan

comments.body:
## Resolution: a two-tier session, with a small core that earns the streak

**The session is three tiers, and only the first is required.**

1. **Warm-up: ~8 quick reps, about 4 minutes. This alone completes the day.**
   Short recall and recognition reps - identify the pattern a problem needs, give the complexity of a snippet, fill in a missing line of a known algorithm, predict what a fragment returns for a given input.
2. **Main exercise: one full problem, roughly 30 minutes. Optional.**
   Offered after the warm-up, and declining it still counts as a completed day.
3. **Open continuation: after the main exercise, keep going with whatever lesson or exercise you like.**
   No cap, no fixed serving beyond tier 1.

**Why the small core is the whole point.**
The minimum session has to be small enough that it is never skipped, because bad days are the only days that matter - good days were never the problem.
A 40-minute minimum is a session you skip when tired, and one skip usually ends the habit.

The warm-up is not filler protecting a streak.
Pattern recognition is the highest-value-per-minute training available for entry-level interviews: recognising "this is a sliding window" in ten seconds matters more than typing a full solution slowly.
The main exercises are how recognition converts into execution.

This also keeps the streak honest, which matters because a single-player streak has no external enforcement.
The streak measures showing up; the exercises measure improving. Conflating the two is what makes self-imposed streaks feel fake.

**The session is domain-agnostic.**
Algorithms are not the only purpose of this app.
Warm-up reps and main exercises both draw from whatever domains are active - algorithms now, SQL close behind, concepts later, front end if it is ever built.
Nothing in the session shape may assume the content is an algorithm problem.
This is a hard requirement on the exercise abstraction, not a later enhancement.

**Sub-questions settled:**

- **Wrong answer on a warm-up rep** - correct it immediately, show the right answer, and re-queue that rep later in the same session. Reps are cheap, so in-session repetition is free.
- **Stuck on a main exercise** - a hint ladder the user chooses to climb: pattern name, then approach, then the key insight, then the solution. Every rung taken is recorded, because "solved after three hints" and "solved cold" are different data points and the scheduler needs to tell them apart.
- **Done for today** - warm-up complete. Nothing more.
- **Fixed serving or open-ended** - a fixed serving followed by an open door. The serving protects the habit; the door lets a good day be a good day.
- **Does partial completion count** - for the streak, yes. For the scheduler, an abandoned exercise is real signal and is recorded as abandoned rather than discarded.

**Calibration confirmed with the captain:** the warm-up reads as genuinely valuable rather than busywork, and four minutes is small enough for a bad day.
comments.author: KyleNaluan

issues.title: Whether Blind 75 problem statements can ship in a public repo
issues.body:
Part of #1

## Question

Can Blind 75 problem statements ship in a public repository, and if not, what is the cheapest lawful source of problem text?

The repo is public and doubles as a portfolio artifact, so this is a real constraint rather than a technicality.
The *list* of problems is almost certainly fine - titles and the fact that a problem is considered interview-relevant are not protectable.
The **problem statements themselves are LeetCode's copyrighted prose**, and copying 75 of them into a public repo is infringement that can get the repo taken down.

Establish, with sources:

1. What is actually protectable here, and what is not.
2. Whether any openly-licensed collection of interview-style problem statements exists that permits reuse, and under what licence and attribution terms.
3. Whether existing open datasets of coding problems (and their test cases) are usable, and how their licences read.
4. The practical fallback: writing fresh statements for known problems. Confirm that describing a well-known problem in original words is clean, and note any pitfalls.
5. Whether keeping the repo public but the problem content private is a workable middle path.

Deliverable is a recommendation with the licence citations behind it, not a general survey.
issues.author: KyleNaluan

comments.body:
## Resolution: public engine, private content - the private-solutions decision already collapsed this question

Full report with citations: `data/swe-license-r4/report.md` (firstmate-local).

**Not legal advice.** Engineering diligence for a low-stakes, single-user personal decision. Nothing in the recommended path warrants a professional; the one circumstance that would is named below.

### The answer

**Ship the engine publicly; keep all problem *content* in the private repo the solutions already go to.**

The ticket was written assuming problem content would live publicly alongside the code.
[The streak decision](https://github.com/KyleNaluan/swe-prep/issues/7) killed that assumption by sending solutions to a separate private repo.
Since the authoring unit is *statement + test cases + reference solution + input generator*, three of those four were already going private. Moving the statement across costs nothing and leaves the public, portfolio-facing repo containing **zero protected prose**.

Concretely:

- **Public `swe-prep`**: the engine (runner, grader, schedulers, UI), the **list of problem titles** (a free fact), and optionally a few **original** demo statements so the format is legible to a portfolio reader.
- **Private content repo**: statements, test data, reference solutions, generators. Loaded by the app via a private submodule or a gitignored local path.

This is also the fastest path to the first daily session, which is the map's binding constraint: no 75-statement authoring project stands between now and drilling.

### What is actually protectable

- **Free to publish:** the list of problems, the titles, the fact that each is interview-relevant, and the underlying algorithmic idea. Ideas, procedures and methods are excluded by 17 U.S.C. §102(b), and facts and plain lists of facts are not copyrightable.
- **Not free:** LeetCode's statement prose, its distinctive worked examples, and its constraint framing - original literary expression - plus any paraphrase close enough to be substantially similar.

### Sources checked, and one trap worth knowing

**No openly-licensed source of Blind 75 / NeetCode 150 statements exists, and none can.** "Blind 75" is a curated list *of LeetCode's problems*. Repos claiming to "have Blind 75" either licence only their author's solution code (e.g. `kamyu104/LeetCode-Solutions`, MIT over the code, not the prose) or reproduce LeetCode text with no right to grant.

**Clean, genuinely reusable datasets** (original-authored, permissive): **HumanEval** (MIT, 164 hand-written problems) and **MBPP** (CC BY 4.0, 974 crowd-sourced). Also **Exercism `problem-specifications`** (MIT, statements plus canonical test data). All are general or entry-level programming katas rather than interview-algorithm curation, so adopting them would mean abandoning the curated set - useful as a format demo, not as the content pile.

**The trap: a permissive wrapper licence does not cure scraped provenance.**
**APPS** ships an MIT `LICENSE` but its 10,000 problems are collected from Codeforces, Kattis, AtCoder and others.
**CodeContests** is Apache 2.0 for code and CC BY 4.0 for non-code, but aggregates problems from Aizu, AtCoder, CodeChef, Codeforces and HackerEarth, and explicitly disclaims that third-party material may carry separate terms.
**Rule: trust a permissive licence only when the licensor authored the statements.** A licensor can only license what they own.

### Writing fresh statements (the fallback, and later polish)

Confirmed clean: because the algorithm is unprotectable, describing a known problem in original words with your own examples and your own generated test data produces a statement you own outright and can publish.

Named pitfalls that turn a clean rewrite dirty:

1. **Paraphrase that is too close** - copyright reaches substantially similar expression. Write from the idea, ideally without the source open, then check the phrasing does not track the original.
2. **Reproducing distinctive examples verbatim** - the specific worked example is part of their expression. Invent your own values.
3. **Copying curated test data** - generate cases from your own reference solution and input generator, which the design already calls for. Self-generated I/O pairs are yours.
4. **Constraint tables and formatting tics** - low risk individually, cumulative in aggregate. Use your own layout.

This is good later work for portfolio polish. It loses as a *gate* purely on time.

### Terms of service, separate from copyright

**LeetCode's ToS forbids crawling, scraping and spidering outright**, independent of the copyright analysis and regardless of whether content lands in a public or private repo.
So "just scrape Blind 75 into the app" is off the table permanently.
It does not bar reading a problem manually and writing your own statement, which uses the service as intended.

*Confidence note from the report: the live terms page was Cloudflare-blocked during research, so this clause is quoted from indexed text rather than re-pulled from origin. Flagged rather than papered over.*

### Residual caveats, honestly stated

Private is not the same as licensed.
Copying a statement into a private file is still technically a reproduction; with no distribution and purely personal single-user use, the practical exposure is negligible. That is **unenforced-and-unexposed in practice, not licensed** - reading practice, not law.

**The one thing that would change the analysis is distribution.**
If problem content ever reaches another person - the shared-instance idea already out of scope on the map - reopen this and lean on fresh original statements or the clean datasets for anything that leaves the machine.
comments.author: KyleNaluan

issues.title: How a submission is judged
issues.body:
Part of #1

## Question

How is a submission judged?

Settle what the app checks when the captain hits run, and what verdicts exist.

At minimum: is it pure pass/fail against test cases, or is there partial credit?
Are there time or memory limits, and are they graded or merely reported?
Does the app say anything about *approach* - complexity, idiomatic style - or only about correctness?
What feedback appears on failure: which case failed, expected versus actual, the input, or something less generous so the captain has to think?

The last one matters more than it looks.
A judge that hands over the failing input immediately trains debugging; one that only says "wrong answer" trains the interview skill of reasoning about your own code without an oracle. That is a deliberate design choice, not an implementation detail.

Also settle whether a submission's result is durable, since the scheduling ticket will need a history of how each attempt went.
issues.author: KyleNaluan

comments.body:
## Resolution: correctness is pass/fail, help is opt-in and recorded, and claimed complexity is verified by measurement

**Correctness verdict.** A submission passes or it does not. No partial credit - it would invent a number that means nothing and soften the only honest signal available. The count of tests passed is shown; it is not a score.

**Failure feedback: withhold by default, reveal on request, record the reveal.**

On failure the app reports only how many tests failed.
Re-reading your own code and reasoning about it without an oracle is the skill a real interview tests, and an app that always hands over the failing case trains the opposite reflex - which is why people grind hundreds of problems and still freeze.
An explicit "show me the failing case" is always available and returns input, expected, and actual.
Using it is **recorded visibly but never penalised**: penalties on a self-imposed system only teach the user to game themselves.

This is deliberately the same shape as the hint ladder for being stuck, so the app has one consistent idea about help: always available, always chosen, always recorded.

**Approach: authored target complexity, self-report first, then empirical verification.**

Correctness is the floor, not the bar - a working brute force gets rejected in a real interview.
Each problem carries an authored target complexity.
After tests pass, the app asks the user to state their solution's time and space complexity **before** revealing the target, because articulating complexity out loud is itself the interview skill.

A self-report alone is unverified and would congratulate an O(n^2) solution claiming to be O(n) - the single case most worth catching.
So the claim is checked by **measuring scaling empirically**: run the submission at growing input sizes and fit the runtime curve.

- This reliably catches polynomial blow-up, which is the error that actually costs interviews.
- It cannot cleanly separate O(n) from O(n log n); constant factors swamp a log at practical sizes. The app must therefore only make coarse claims, and where measurement is inconclusive it must say "measured scaling is consistent with your claim" rather than "correct".
- It makes the self-report a **prediction scored against measurement** rather than an honour-system checkbox, which is a stronger training loop.

Costs accepted, and they are real:

- Every problem needs a **large-input generator** in addition to correctness cases. This lands on the content-authoring pile, which is already the most likely place this project stalls.
- Timing on a normal machine is noisy - usable for order-of-magnitude differences, useless for anything finer.
- The runner needs a **second execution mode** that runs a submission at multiple input sizes and captures timings. This is a requirement on the exercise/runner abstraction.

**Style feedback: none.** Automated style nagging is noise and is not what interviews reject people over.

**Resource limits: reported, not graded.** A generous timeout catches infinite loops; runtime is shown for interest. Grading on wall-clock would punish JVM warm-up and teach nothing.

**Durable results: every attempt is persisted, not just the final verdict.** Each records pass/fail, submissions taken, hint-ladder rungs climbed, whether the failing case was revealed, the complexity self-assessment and what measurement said about it, and whether the exercise was abandoned. This history is the scheduler's input, and thin records here would quietly cripple that ticket.

**Deliberately left open for later:** supplementing measurement with LLM code analysis. See the map's "Not yet specified".
comments.author: KyleNaluan

issues.title: The exercise and runner abstraction
issues.body:
Part of #1

## Question

Design the exercise and runner abstraction.

This is the seam that decides whether the captain's two stated requirements - interchangeable languages, and practice across SWE domains beyond algorithms - are cheap or impossible later.

Define the model: what an exercise *is*, independent of language and domain; what a test specification looks like; what contract a runner adapter satisfies; and how a submission flows from editor to verdict.

It must hold, without redesign:

- **Java** (the v1 default) and at least one other language, proving the language seam is real rather than aspirational.
- **SQL**, where the "runner" is an embedded engine, the fixture is a schema plus seed data, and the verdict is a result-set comparison. This ships close behind v1, so it is a design requirement now.
- **Front end** at least conceptually, where grading means DOM and interaction assertions in a headless browser. Not being built, but the abstraction should not make it impossible.
- **Concepts and flashcards**, a later phase with no execution at all. Make sure "exercise" does not secretly mean "thing that runs code".
- **Warm-up reps** (settled by [the daily-session ticket](https://github.com/KyleNaluan/swe-prep/issues/3)): very short, non-execution, answerable in seconds - pattern identification, complexity of a snippet, fill-in-a-missing-line, predict-the-output. These are a first-class exercise kind, not a special case bolted on, and they exist in every domain. Roughly eight of them are the required daily core, so they are the most-used thing in the app.

The session that consumes this model is domain-agnostic: nothing may assume an exercise is an algorithm problem.
A hint ladder (pattern name, approach, key insight, solution) and a record of which rung was reached are part of the model, since the scheduler distinguishes "solved cold" from "solved after three hints", and an abandoned attempt is recorded rather than discarded.

**A second execution mode is required** (settled by [the judging ticket](https://github.com/KyleNaluan/swe-prep/issues/5)): besides running a submission against correctness cases, the runner must run it at multiple growing input sizes and capture timings, so a claimed complexity can be checked against measured scaling. Design the runner contract to carry this from the start rather than bolting it on.

**The runner must sit behind a swappable interface** (settled by [the platform ticket](https://github.com/KyleNaluan/swe-prep/issues/2)): a local-process runner today, a sandboxed container runner if the app is ever hosted. That swap must not require touching the exercise model. Hosting is a protected future goal, so this costs nothing now and is expensive to retrofit.

**Every row belonging to a person carries a user id**, with exactly one user seeded and no authentication built. Ownership threaded through the model from the start is what makes adding auth later a day's work instead of a refactor.

Beware the two failure modes: hardcoding Java assumptions into the schema, and over-abstracting into something so generic it expresses nothing.
Use `/domain-modeling` to pin the vocabulary, since these terms will be load-bearing across the whole build.
issues.author: KyleNaluan

comments.body:
## Resolution: split Grader from Runner, and make test cases language-neutral data

### The trap this avoids

The obvious design makes `Exercise` mean "thing that runs code", after which concepts and warm-up reps become special cases bolted on the side.
The fix is separating two things that are usually conflated: **what the user produces** and **how it is judged**.

### The core split

**A `Grader` decides pass or fail. A `Runner` only executes.** Everything else follows from keeping those apart.

- A concept question has a Grader and **no Runner at all**.
- A Java problem and a SQL query both need a Runner, but entirely different Graders.
- A front-end exercise, if ever built, is a different Grader over a browser Runner.

This is what stops "exercise" from secretly meaning "code".

### The model

- **`Exercise`** - the authored unit of practice. Prompt, domain, topic tags, difficulty, an ordered hint ladder, a response spec, a grading spec.
- **`Form`** - `Rep` (seconds; the required daily core) or `Challenge` (~30 minutes). **An attribute, not a separate type.** It decides where an exercise appears in a session and nothing else. This is what lets warm-up reps exist in every domain instead of being an algorithms-only gimmick.
- **`Response`** - what the user produces: `Choice`, `ShortAnswer`, `Program`, `Query`, and later `Component`.
- **`Runner`** - the swappable execution boundary. Takes sources, an entrypoint, an input and limits; returns output, timings and exit status. A local-process runner today, a container runner if the app is ever hosted. **Graders never know which.**
- **`Attempt`** - the durable record: user id, exercise, hint-ladder rungs climbed, whether the failing case was revealed, the complexity claim, measured scaling, and the outcome including abandonment.
- **`Submission`** - one press of run, within an attempt.

### The decision that makes languages cheap

**Test cases are data, not code.**

```
input:    [[2,7,11,15], 9]
expected: [0,1]
```

Language-neutral JSON.
The **language adapter** supplies the harness that deserialises that into the target language's types, calls the user's function, and serialises the result back.
A test case is authored **once** and runs in every language ever added.

The failure this avoids: writing test cases as JUnit means every new language requires re-authoring the entire problem set. That is the difference between pluggable languages being real and being aspirational.

The same move applies to the function signature - the exercise declares it in language-neutral types, and each adapter generates the stub and harness. This is how LeetCode supports twenty languages.

**Accepted constraint:** this restricts exercises to problems with JSON-representable inputs and outputs. Most of Blind 75 qualifies. Trees and linked lists need a serialisation convention, and **LeetCode's existing convention is adopted rather than inventing one** (`[1,2,3,null,4]`), since the captain will be reading their problem statements anyway.

### How each domain lands

| Domain | Response | Runner | Grader |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Algorithms | `Program` | language adapter | run against cases, compare output |
| SQL | `Query` | embedded engine | apply fixture, run, compare result set |
| Concepts / reps | `Choice` or `ShortAnswer` | **none** | compare to key |
| Front end (later) | `Component` | headless browser | DOM and interaction assertions |

Front end is the one place the JSON-test-case model does **not** extend, and this is stated plainly rather than papered over.
It does not need to: `Component` carries its own spec shape, because `Grader` and `Runner` are both polymorphic.
The abstraction's obligation is to not foreclose front end, and it does not.

### Complexity measurement

Deliberately a separate concern.
An exercise **may** carry an `InputGenerator` and a target complexity.
When present, a `ScalingProbe` invokes the same Runner repeatedly at growing input sizes and returns a timing curve, per the judging decision.
Exercises without a generator are simply never checked - it is optional metadata rather than a required field, so it never pollutes the concepts layer.

### Ownership

Every row belonging to a person carries a user id, with exactly one user seeded and no authentication built, per the platform decision.

issues.title: What makes a single-player streak actually stick
issues.body:
Part of #1

## Question

What makes a single-player streak actually stick?

This is the hardest design question on the map, and the one the project most likely fails on.

Duolingo's product is the streak, not the teaching, but its mechanics lean heavily on things swe-prep does not have: other people, leagues, loss aversion against a public record, and push notifications from a party that is not you.
Here the captain is the only user *and* the author.
He knows the XP is invented, he can edit the database, and he can turn off any nag he writes.
Self-imposed points do not create obligation.

Settle what actually generates the pull to open it tomorrow.
Candidates worth weighing rather than assuming: a genuinely public streak, since the repo is public and the commit graph is real external evidence; stakes with a real cost to missing; progress measured against something true (readiness against real interview criteria) rather than invented currency; making the *session* intrinsically satisfying enough that it needs no external hook; and scheduled surfacing so the decision to practise is not made fresh each day.

Be blunt about which of these are known-weak. A mechanic that only works because the captain agrees to pretend it works is not a mechanic.
issues.author: KyleNaluan

comments.body:
## Resolution: no invented currency - a true external record, an honest readiness picture, and a streak that survives a bad evening

### Start with the uncomfortable part

Duolingo's streak runs on other people's leagues, loss aversion against a public record, and notifications from a party that is not you.
swe-prep has none of that: the captain is the only user *and* the author, he knows the points are invented, and he can edit the database.

**Invented currency is therefore cut entirely. No XP, no hearts, no lives, no leagues.**
Any number the captain can print himself is a number he stops believing in around week two, and a fake number that goes up is actively misleading about whether he is getting hired.

What the design *can* do is narrower and more honest: **remove every excuse, make the record true rather than invented, and make breaking it cost something real.**

### 1. Commit real solutions - to a PRIVATE repo

Every solved problem is committed, so the GitHub contribution graph becomes a real, external, permanent record that the app did not invent and the captain cannot fake. A skipped week is a visible hole.

**Solutions go to a private repo, with "include private contributions on my profile" enabled.**
The green squares still appear publicly; nobody can see what is behind them.

The captain declined publishing solutions, and that instinct is right for a second reason: a public dump of Blind 75 solutions reads as interview grinding rather than building, and it would collide with [the licensing question](https://github.com/KyleNaluan/swe-prep/issues/4) if statements ride along.

Nothing that mattered is lost - the record is still external, permanent, and publicly visible as activity. The witness function was never about anyone reading the solutions.

The two purposes separate cleanly: **swe-prep itself is the portfolio piece** - a real Spring Boot application with a defensible design, far better evidence than 75 solved puzzles - while the contribution graph is purely the habit mechanic.

**Hard rule: commit real artifacts only, never synthetic "practice happened" markers.** Auto-inflating a contribution graph is gaming, and the captain would know.

### 2. A true readiness picture instead of XP

This also resolves the map's open question about what "ready for interviews" means; the two were the same question about what the captain sees when he opens the app.

Instead of a score, the honest state of things:

```
Patterns covered: 8 of 12 - Shaky: graphs, intervals
Not touched in 3 weeks: dynamic programming
Solved cold on first attempt: 19 of 41
```

Every figure derives from the attempt records [judging](https://github.com/KyleNaluan/swe-prep/issues/5) and [scheduling](https://github.com/KyleNaluan/swe-prep/issues/8) already keep, so it costs nothing to compute and all of it is **true**.
It creates pull because it is specific and honest about something the captain actually wants, not because it is a game.

### 3. A scheduled cue

The decision to practise must not be made fresh each day.
A notification at a chosen time, which is nearly free on this machine (scheduled nudges already run here).
Habit research is consistent that the cue matters more than the motivation.

### 4. The streak as a record, not a currency

Days practised, shown next to readiness. It is true, so it is fine to display. It is not spendable, and nothing is denominated in it.

### 5. A capped repair mechanic

Duolingo's streak freeze exists for a real reason: an all-or-nothing streak that breaks makes people quit outright rather than resume.
A missed day may be repaired by a double session the next day, **capped at roughly two per month** so it stays meaningful.
This preserves the asset across one bad evening, which is exactly when habits die.

### Ruled out

**Financial stakes** (Beeminder-style). They genuinely work, but wiring up money is real friction, and adding a punishment to an activity already being avoided is more likely to increase the avoidance. Available later if nothing else lands.

### The lever that beats everything in this ticket

**Tell one person.**
Accountability to an actual human is the strongest effect in the habit literature and nothing in-app comes close.
The record already exists; one friend who occasionally asks would outperform every mechanic above combined.
This cannot be built, which is exactly why it is written down.

### Closing note for whoever picks this up later

**If this design does not get the captain practising, the answer is not more gamification.**
It would mean something outside the app is wrong, and building more mechanics in response would be the expensive mistake.

issues.title: How the app chooses what you practise next
issues.body:
Part of #1

## Question

How does the app choose what the captain practises next?

The map's whole premise is that re-solving the right problems on a schedule beats grinding new ones, so the scheduler is where the learning value actually lives.

Settle the selection model: spaced repetition on a known algorithm (SM-2, FSRS, or a simpler interval ladder), a weakness-targeting model driven by past results, coverage of topic categories, or some combination.
Decide what signal feeds it - pass/fail, attempts taken, time spent, self-rated difficulty - and reconcile that with what the judging ticket decided is actually recorded.

Two specifics to resolve rather than leave implicit:

1. Spaced-repetition algorithms were built for flashcards, where a review takes seconds. A hard algorithm problem takes 40 minutes. Whether the standard intervals survive that difference is a real question, not a detail.
2. What happens with a problem the captain has never seen, versus one he has failed twice, versus one he has passed cleanly three times. The cold-start and the graduation behaviour both need an answer.
issues.author: KyleNaluan

comments.body:
## Resolution: two schedulers over one shared record - a due-date queue for reps, a priority score for challenges

### Why one scheduler cannot serve both

Spaced repetition assumes reviews are cheap.
Anki works because twenty due cards cost four minutes.
That arithmetic breaks completely for a 30-40 minute `Challenge`: twenty due challenges is a fortnight of work, and a scheduler that generates impossible debt is one that gets ignored within a week.

The scarcity is also structural.
Roughly 90 challenge slots exist in three months of daily practice, against ~75 problems.
There is barely room for one pass, let alone spaced review, and the scheduler must respect that rather than pretend otherwise.

### Reps: a due-date queue

Reps cost seconds, so standard spaced repetition applies exactly as designed - eight due today is four minutes.

SM-2 is about fifty lines and entirely adequate for one user and ~400 reps.
FSRS is better on paper, but the difference is marginal at this scale.
**Keep the algorithm swappable** and do not agonise over the choice.

### Challenges: a priority score, not a due date

Each day the scheduler answers one question: *what is the single best use of forty minutes today?*

Score every problem on:

- time since last attempt (raises priority)
- how badly the last attempt went (raises priority)
- whether its pattern is under-covered (raises priority)
- a **hard floor on minimum interval** - re-solving something from two days ago is memorisation, not learning

Take the highest scorer.

Due dates ask what is *owed*; a priority score asks what is *worth it*. Only the second survives scarcity.

### The signal

[Judging](https://github.com/KyleNaluan/swe-prep/issues/5) leaves a rich per-attempt record.
**Collapse it into a single 0-5 quality score** rather than feeding raw fields into either algorithm:

- Passed on the first submission, no hints, no failing-case reveal, complexity claim correct → **5**
- Passed, but climbed the hint ladder or revealed the failing case → **3**
- Failed or abandoned → **1**

This maps directly onto SM-2 and keeps the scheduler from ossifying around today's exact set of recorded fields.
For reps, correct-or-not plus the "asked why" confidence signal from [the warm-up rep decision](https://github.com/KyleNaluan/swe-prep/issues/9) feeds the same scale.

**Time taken is deliberately excluded.**
It is tempting and it is noise: interruptions, thinking before typing, and typing fast on a misunderstood problem all corrupt it. It would add variance without carrying information.

### New versus review

The classic failure is Anki's - unbounded new material, review debt piles up, the user quits.

**Review debt first, new problems second, with a weekly cap on introductions.**
If something genuinely weak is due, the challenge slot goes to it; otherwise a new problem is introduced.
The cap matters because ~75 problems can be burned through in two months, arriving at breadth with no depth and everything half-remembered.

**Nothing is ever deleted.**
A problem passed cleanly three times earns an interval of months. That is retirement, not removal.

### "Interview soon" mode

In the final fortnight before interviews the objective genuinely changes: broad recency beats optimal long-term spacing, especially across weak patterns.

This is a different scoring function, not a different app.
It re-weights the challenge priority score toward broad recency and drops the minimum-interval floor.
Cheap to build, and the difference between a tool that trains the captain and one that also prepares him for a specific date.

### Note for the domain layer

Once SQL exercises exist, the daily rep set should mix domains rather than running as separate per-domain queues.
The scheduler operates over exercises, and `domain` is one more coverage dimension alongside topic - not a reason for a second queue.

issues.title: What a warm-up rep is, across domains
issues.body:
Part of #1

## Question

What is a warm-up rep, concretely, in each domain - and how are they authored?

The daily-session ticket settled that ~8 warm-up reps of about four minutes are the required daily core.
That makes them the most-used surface in the entire app, and the thing that has to carry the habit.
It also makes them a content-authoring problem roughly the size of the main problem set, which is currently unaccounted for.

Settle:

1. **The rep types.** Pattern identification, complexity of a snippet, fill in a missing line, predict the output were the sketch. Confirm, cut, or extend that list, and define what each actually presents and accepts as an answer.
2. **Per domain.** What a rep looks like for algorithms, for SQL, and for the later concepts layer. They should feel like one system rather than three bolted together.
3. **Answer format and grading.** Multiple choice grades trivially but trains recognition only; free text trains recall but is harder to grade. Decide per rep type rather than globally, and be explicit about which are which.
4. **Authoring.** Where reps come from. Derived automatically from the problem set, hand-written, LLM-drafted and verified, or some mix. Roughly how many are needed before the app stops repeating itself uncomfortably, and whether that count is reachable.
5. **The relationship to main exercises.** Whether a rep is generated from a problem the captain has already attempted, or authored independently of the problem set.

Resist the pull to make reps a thin quiz layer.
Their value claim is that recognition is the highest-value-per-minute interview training there is, and they only earn the daily slot if they actually deliver that.
issues.author: KyleNaluan

comments.body:
## Resolution: five rep types, mostly multiple choice, nearly all derived from the problem set

### The rep types

1. **Pattern identification** - a problem statement, pick the pattern. The highest-value type, because recognising the shape is the actual entry-level interview skill.
2. **Complexity of a snippet** - given code, give its time/space complexity.
3. **Fill in the missing line** - an algorithm core with a blank.
4. **Predict the output** - what does this fragment return for this input.
5. **Spot the bug** - subtly wrong code, identify the defect.

Spot-the-bug is added to the original sketch deliberately.
It is code review, which is genuinely the job, and it coheres with [the judging decision](https://github.com/KyleNaluan/swe-prep/issues/5) to make the captain reason about code without an oracle. This trains exactly that, in about twenty seconds.

### Answer format and grading

**Multiple choice by default; predict-the-output is free text.**

- **Complexity** - multiple choice from a fixed ladder. The answer set is finite, so this grades exactly; free text would only mean normalising `O(n^2)` against `O(n squared)` for no benefit.
- **Pattern identification** - multiple choice; roughly a dozen possible answers.
- **Spot the bug** - multiple choice, or selecting the offending line.
- **Fill in the missing line** - multiple choice among plausible lines, including realistic wrong ones (an off-by-one, a flipped comparison). Executing a typed line was considered and rejected: a Java compile takes a second or two and eight of those destroys the four-minute session. Discrimination is the target anyway.
- **Predict the output** - free text, exact match after normalisation. The answer is a concrete value, so it grades exactly as typed.

**Stated plainly: reps train recognition and discrimination. Production is what the `Challenge` exercises are for.**
That is a division of labour rather than a compromise, and it is the honest answer to whether reps are busywork - they are not attempting to replace writing code.

**Authoring standard that follows: the distractors are the entire value.**
A rep with three obviously-wrong options teaches nothing and wastes a slot in a four-minute daily budget. Plausible wrong answers are the product.

### Explanations

Every rep carries a short explanation of the correct answer.

- **Shown immediately on a wrong answer.** That is the teaching moment; the right answer without the reason teaches almost nothing.
- **Not shown by default on a correct answer.** Re-reading something already known is low-value compared to retrieval, and eight explanations would roughly double the session, attacking the property the whole design protects.
- **Always one keystroke away.** Some correct answers are lucky guesses and the captain knows it at the time.
- **Asking is recorded.** "Correct, and asked why" is a different data point from "correct, moved on", and is a free behavioural read on confidence. Flashcard systems normally buy this signal by interrupting with "how hard was that?", which users learn to click through. Here the same signal comes from behaviour that would happen anyway, and the scheduler can resurface the rep sooner without ever asking a question.

Explanations are generated in the same pass as the rep, so marginal cost is near zero.
**They are verified alongside the rep rather than trusted** - a confidently wrong explanation is worse than none.

### Authoring: reps derive from the problem set

The naive read is that reps are a second content pile the size of the first, and that pile is where this project most plausibly dies.
That mostly dissolves: **nearly every rep is derived from a problem already being authored.**

Per problem, roughly:

- one **pattern-ID** rep, from the statement
- one or two **complexity** reps, from the reference solution and a brute-force variant
- one or two **fill-in-the-blank** reps, from the reference solution
- one **spot-the-bug** rep, by mutating the reference solution - near-mechanical, since the mutation *is* the answer
- one **predict-output** rep, by running the reference on a small input

That is five to six reps per problem, so ~75 problems yields roughly **400 reps**, LLM-drafted and human-verified.
Eight reps a day is about 240 slots a month, so that pool is comfortably sufficient - and note that repetition is the *point* under spaced repetition, so "how soon does it repeat" is the wrong question.

**Consequence for the content model: the reference solution is the seed for everything.**
The real authoring unit is statement + test cases + reference solution + input generator, and the reps fall out of it.
There is one content pile, not two.

### Gating and cold start

Some rep types only make sense once the captain has met the problem.
Pattern identification works cold - that is the point of it.
Fill-in-the-blank on a solution never seen is guessing, not practice.

So derived reps unlock as problems are attempted.
This looks like a cold-start problem and is not: **on day one, ~75 pattern-ID reps are available**, the highest-value type, which is weeks of daily cores by itself.
The pool deepens as problems are solved, and the reps that appear concern problems actually wrestled with - which is what spaced repetition should be doing.

The app gets richer the more it is used.

issues.title: What a SQL exercise actually looks like
issues.body:
Part of #1

## Question

What does a SQL exercise actually look like?

The [exercise abstraction](https://github.com/KyleNaluan/swe-prep/issues/6) settled the shape - a `Query` response, an embedded engine as the Runner, and a Grader that applies a fixture, runs the query, and compares result sets.
This ticket fills that in, because SQL ships close behind the Java algorithms in v1 and is the first real proof that the domain seam works.

Settle:

1. **The engine.** The app's own state is Postgres. Exercise fixtures need to be disposable and reset per attempt, which is a different requirement. Decide whether exercises run against the same Postgres (schema-per-attempt, or a transaction rolled back), a separate throwaway database, or an embedded engine. Note that dialect matters: practising SQLite dialect while interviewing on Postgres would train the wrong thing.
2. **The fixture format.** Schema plus seed data, authored per exercise or shared across a set. Sharing one realistic schema across many exercises is cheaper to author and closer to real work; per-exercise fixtures are more isolated. Pick one and say why.
3. **Result comparison.** Whether row order matters (it does not, unless the exercise asked for `ORDER BY`), how column naming and ordering are treated, and how a near-miss is reported given the judging decision to withhold detail by default.
4. **What is actually tested.** Entry-level SQL interviews lean on joins, aggregation, grouping, and window functions rather than exotica. Decide the topic list and roughly how many exercises make it worth having.
5. **Warm-up reps for SQL.** Per the daily-session decision, reps exist in every domain. Decide what a seconds-long SQL rep is - reading a query and predicting its output, spotting why a join drops rows, identifying which clause is wrong. Coordinate with the [warm-up rep ticket](https://github.com/KyleNaluan/swe-prep/issues/9).
6. **Whether SQL exercises carry a complexity target.** Almost certainly not in the algorithmic sense, but query plans are a real interview topic. Decide whether that is in scope or explicitly not.
issues.author: KyleNaluan

comments.body:
## Resolution: a Postgres fixture database, a few shared schemas, and multiset result comparison

### Engine: the same Postgres, a separate fixture database, per-attempt transaction rollback

**Dialect parity is the deciding factor.**
SQLite or H2 would be easier to embed and would train the captain on a dialect he will not interview in - window function syntax, `FULL OUTER JOIN`, and type handling all differ in ways that bite in a real interview.
Postgres is already running for app state, so there is no infrastructure to add.

Each attempt runs inside a transaction that is rolled back, which gives perfect isolation at zero cost and handles exercises that write as well as those that only read.

**The submission connects as a read-only role** on the fixture database, so a query containing `DROP TABLE` is refused outright rather than merely rolled back.

The app's own state database and the exercise fixture database are separate concerns and stay separate.

### Fixtures: two or three shared schemas, many exercises each

Realistic shapes - an e-commerce schema (users, orders, products, order_items) and perhaps an events/analytics schema - with seed data, and many exercises authored against each.

Per-exercise fixtures sound cleaner and are worse in practice: most of a 30-minute budget would go on re-reading an unfamiliar schema instead of writing SQL.
A shared schema is learned once and then answers twenty questions, which is how real SQL interviews run and how the job actually works.

It is also what makes SQL warm-up reps viable at all - a twenty-second rep is only possible against tables already known.

### Result comparison

**Compare result sets as a multiset of rows, matching columns by position and ignoring column names.**
Row order is ignored unless the exercise explicitly asked for ordering, which is a per-exercise flag.

- Ignoring names avoids failing the captain over a cosmetic alias.
- Matching by position still holds him to "return name, then total" as asked.
- **A normalisation pass is required** for numeric types (`int` vs `numeric`), float rounding, and NULL handling, or false failures will be constant and maddening.

**Minimal failure signal, under the withhold-by-default rule from [judging](https://github.com/KyleNaluan/swe-prep/issues/5):**

```
Your result: 12 rows. Expected: 8.
```

This is the exact analogue of "3 of 12 tests failed" and is unusually diagnostic for SQL without giving anything away - a row count above expected almost always means join fan-out, and that is a pattern worth learning to see instantly.
Reveal-on-request shows the actual diff.

### What is tested

Joins, including why a `LEFT JOIN` silently drops rows; aggregation with `GROUP BY` and `HAVING`; subqueries and CTEs; window functions (`row_number`, `rank`, `lag`); NULL semantics; finding duplicates; date bucketing; and top-N-per-group.

**Roughly 25-40 exercises.** SQL is a much smaller surface than algorithms and does not need parity with the problem set.

### SQL warm-up reps

The five rep types from [the warm-up rep decision](https://github.com/KyleNaluan/swe-prep/issues/9) map over with one substitution: complexity does not apply, so predict-the-output takes that slot.

**Spot-the-bug is the standout type here, more so than in algorithms.**
Most real SQL errors are silently wrong rather than syntax errors - a missing `GROUP BY` column, `HAVING` where `WHERE` belonged, a join fanning out and quietly doubling totals, a `= NULL` that matches nothing.
Those are exactly the defects that reach production, and twenty seconds of pattern-matching against them is high value.

Reps derive from the reference query, exactly as they derive from the reference solution for algorithms. There is still one content pile.

### Complexity and query plans

**No complexity target for SQL exercises** - no input generator, no scaling probe. The [abstraction](https://github.com/KyleNaluan/swe-prep/issues/6) made that metadata optional precisely for this case.

**Query plans are deferred, not built.**
A real interview topic but shallow at entry level, and grading on `EXPLAIN` output is a research project rather than a feature.
If it ever happens it belongs as a rep type ("which of these uses the index?"), not a graded exercise. Logged as fog on the map.

issues.body:
## Parent

Part of the planning map: #1

## What to build

**This is the tracer bullet, and it is deliberately not split.** It proves the riskiest design decision on the map: that a test case authored once as language-neutral JSON can be executed in any language via a generated harness.

From the user's point of view: open the app, see one problem statement and a Monaco editor with a Java method stub, write a solution, press run, and get back a verdict of the form `N of M tests passed`.

Behind that, the test cases are **language-neutral JSON data** (`input` and `expected`), and a Java language adapter generates the harness that deserialises the JSON into Java types, calls the submission, and serialises the result back for comparison. The exercise, its statement, its stub and its cases may be hardcoded in this ticket - loading real content is the next one.

Resist splitting this into "set up Monaco", "add the runner", "wire the endpoint". Those are horizontal slices that each look complete while proving nothing. The design is only tested end to end.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A Java submission written in the browser is compiled and executed on the backend, with no container or sandbox (there is no untrusted code - single user by design)
- [ ] Test cases are stored as language-neutral JSON with `input` and `expected`, containing no Java-specific syntax
- [ ] The Java harness and method stub are generated from a language-neutral signature declaration, not hand-written for this problem
- [ ] The verdict returned is a count of passing tests; a compile error is reported as such and distinguished from a test failure
- [ ] Execution has a generous timeout that catches an infinite loop without failing a slow-but-correct solution
- [ ] A report in the PR describes how well the language-neutral test-case design actually held, including anything that had to be worked around

issues.title: Complexity: self-report, target reveal, and scaling measurement
issues.body:
## Parent

Part of the planning map: #1

## What to build

After tests pass, the app asks you to state your solution's time and space complexity **before** revealing the authored target, because articulating complexity is itself the interview skill.

A self-report alone is unverified and would congratulate an O(n^2) solution claiming to be O(n) - the single case most worth catching. So the claim is checked by **measuring scaling empirically**: the runner executes the submission at growing input sizes and the curve is fitted.

This reliably catches polynomial blow-up, which is the error that costs interviews. It cannot separate O(n) from O(n log n), because constant factors swamp a log at practical sizes. **The app must therefore only make coarse claims**, and say "measured scaling is consistent with your claim" rather than "correct" where measurement is inconclusive.

Exercises without an input generator simply are not checked; the metadata is optional by design.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The user states a complexity before the target is revealed, and cannot see the target first
- [ ] The runner supports a second execution mode that runs a submission at multiple growing input sizes and captures timings
- [ ] A quadratic solution claiming linear complexity is reliably caught and reported
- [ ] Where measurement is inconclusive the app says so explicitly and never asserts correctness
- [ ] An exercise with no input generator skips the check entirely without error
- [ ] The claim and the measurement result are both recorded on the attempt

issues.title: Teach the grader what "equal" means: comparison rules, numeric equality, and an untruncatable result
issues.body:
## Parent

Part of the planning map: #1

## What to build

Teach the grader what "equal" means. Three findings from the tracer bullet (#13) share one root cause: grading is exact JSON equality, and exact equality cannot express the ways two answers can both be correct.

**1. There is no way to say "any valid answer".**

Two Sum accepts `[0,1]` and `[1,0]`. The case format can only name one, so the tracer bullet had to pin an ordering convention into the problem statement to make grading work. That is a workaround written into content to compensate for a gap in the model, and it will recur constantly - "any valid pair", "any order", "any of these shortest paths" describe a large share of interview problems.

An exercise must be able to declare how its answers should be compared. At minimum: exact, order-insensitive for a sequence, and set equality. Design the declaration so a genuinely problem-specific rule is possible later without another redesign.

**Once this exists, remove the ordering convention from the Two Sum statement** and let the exercise declare order-insensitivity instead. That reversal is the proof this ticket worked.

**2. Comparison is numeric-type-sensitive.**

A whole number written one way is not equal to the same number written another. Two Sum is unaffected because everything in it is an integer, but a correct solution returning a wider numeric type where the expected value parses narrower would be graded wrong. Whoever hits it will be told their correct answer is incorrect and have no way to see why, which is the worst possible failure for a study tool.

**3. A correct solution that prints a lot is graded as an error.**

Captured output is capped at 1MB to stop a runaway print loop exhausting memory - a real fix for a real risk. But the cap truncates from the end and the harness reports its result last, so a solution that prints more than the cap and then returns correctly loses its result line and grades as an error rather than showing its pass count.

The cap must stay. Move the result off the same channel as the submission's own output - a separate stream or a result file - so it can never be truncated away by the thing it is measuring.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An exercise can declare how its answers are compared, covering at least exact, order-insensitive sequence, and set equality
- [ ] Two Sum accepts both valid orderings, and the ordering convention is removed from its statement
- [ ] Numerically equal answers grade as equal regardless of how the number is written, with a test that would fail under the old behaviour
- [ ] A solution printing more than the output cap and returning correctly is graded on its results, not as an error
- [ ] The output cap remains, and a runaway print loop still cannot exhaust backend memory
- [ ] Nothing beyond grading comparison is changed; this is not an opening to start content loading or persistence

issues.title: The app silently breaks when Vite does not get port 5173: single hardcoded CORS origin
issues.body:
## Parent

Part of the planning map: #1. Found in real use immediately after #14 landed.

## What's wrong

The app breaks completely if the Vite dev server does not get port 5173, and the failure does not explain itself.

Vite falls back to 5174 whenever 5173 is taken - by another project, a previous run, or an orphaned process. The page then loads normally and every API call is refused by the browser, because the backend allows exactly one origin:

- `WebConfig` defaults `sweprep.web.allowed-origin` to `http://localhost:5173`
- `application.yml` hardcodes the actuator's `management.endpoints.web.cors.allowed-origins` to the same literal

The result is an app that looks like it started fine and then does nothing, with no message naming the real cause. Vite prints its port change as ordinary startup noise, so there is nothing connecting the two. This actually happened on first real use.

The same single-origin assumption also blocks the tailnet access the map calls for: reaching the app from another device means a different origin, which is refused for exactly this reason. So this is not only a dev-machine annoyance - it stands between the app and being usable from anywhere but this one machine.

Note the property is already overridable. The problem is the default plus the silence, not the absence of a knob.

## What to build

Make the port and origin story robust, and make the failure legible when it still happens.

Worth considering rather than prescribing: pinning Vite to a port with `strictPort` so it fails loudly instead of silently moving; having the frontend talk to the backend through a Vite proxy so browser-side calls are same-origin and CORS stops being load-bearing in development; and allowing the tailnet origin so the app is reachable off this machine.

Whatever the approach, a rejected origin must produce a message a person can act on, rather than an app that silently does nothing.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Starting the frontend when 5173 is occupied either fails immediately with a clear message, or works correctly on the port it does get - never starts and silently cannot reach the backend
- [ ] The backend's allowed origin is not a hardcoded single localhost literal in two separate places
- [ ] The app is reachable from another device over the tailnet, per the map's local + tailnet goal
- [ ] A blocked or failed API call surfaces a message naming the cause, instead of an empty or unexplained screen
- [ ] `./test.sh` stays green

issues.body:
## Parent

Part of the planning map: #1.

## What's wrong

An explanation is a first-class requirement of the content design, and there is nowhere to put one.

Every check is meant to carry an explanation of why the correct answer is correct: **shown automatically on a wrong answer, one keystroke away on a correct one, with asking recorded as a confidence signal.** The loader has no such field. issues.title: Choice options are served in file order, so answer position is exploitable
issues.body:
## The problem

Choice options are served and rendered in the order they appear in the content file, and nothing shuffles them. So a learner can exploit answer position instead of knowing the material.

This is not hypothetical. In the first authored AI/ML batch (swe-prep-content PR #4), **all 12 machine-graded multiple-choice questions had the correct answer as option 1**. A blind reviewer who had never seen the answer key noticed the pattern independently - which is exactly how a real learner would notice it, and then pass every question in the batch without understanding any of them.

The authoring gate landed under #42 makes each *distractor* competitive, but says nothing about where the correct answer sits. A set of individually excellent distractors is still worthless if the key is always in the same slot.

## Why fix it in the engine rather than the authoring checklist

The same argument #42 settled: "declared" is a machine question, "plausible" is a human one. Position is entirely mechanical, so it should not depend on an author remembering to vary it, or on a reviewer counting. An author drafting a batch in one sitting will naturally write the correct answer first and then invent wrong ones - the bias is a by-product of how authoring actually happens, so it will recur.

Shuffling at serve or render time makes position bias structurally impossible for all existing and future content, including content authored before this lands.

## Why this is safe to do

Grading already matches the answer key by **text**, not by index (`AnswerKeyGrader`, and `ExerciseParser.matchesKey` uses the same rule when classifying distractors at load time). Display order therefore has no bearing on correctness.

Authored explanations reference options by their content, not by position ("the product and the max do not have that property"), so shuffling does not break them. Confirm this holds rather than assuming it, and if any content or copy does depend on position, that is a content bug to report.

## What to decide

- **Where to shuffle** - serving the exercise, or rendering it. Consider what happens across a page refresh or a resumed session: an order that changes under the learner mid-question is its own usability problem, so a per-attempt stable order is likely wanted rather than a fresh shuffle on every render.
- **Determinism for tests.** Tests that assert on option order will need a seam. Prefer an injectable/seedable source of randomness over disabling the shuffle in test config, so the shipped path is the tested path.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Choice options are not presented in file order; a learner cannot exploit answer position
- [ ] The order a learner sees is stable for the duration of an attempt, not re-shuffled under them
- [ ] Grading is unaffected, since the key matches by text
- [ ] The shuffle is deterministic under test via an explicit seam, not switched off
- [ ] A test proves a question whose key is authored first is not always presented first
- [ ] `./test.sh` green
issues.author: KyleNaluan
