issues.title: The correct answer is the longest option in every authored check, which is a second exploitable tell
issues.body:
## The problem

In the first authored AI/ML batch (swe-prep-content PR #4), the correct answer was the **longest option in all 12** multiple-choice checks, often by a wide margin - 175 characters against a next-longest of 79 on one, 100 against 46 on another. Measured, not eyeballed:

```
aiml-metrics-auc          correct_len=175  lens=[175, 59, 79, 54]
aiml-metrics-f1           correct_len=100  lens=[100, 44, 32, 46]
aiml-tvt-preprocess-leak  correct_len=152  lens=[152, 108, 88, 93]
...12 of 12, correct answer strictly longest or tied
```

A learner who reads none of the questions can score close to full marks by picking the longest, most fully-qualified-sounding option every time.

This is a **sibling of #59 but not fixed by it.** Shuffling positions defeats "always pick the first"; it does nothing about "always pick the longest," because length travels with the option text.

## Why it recurs, and why a checklist won't hold

It is a by-product of how authoring actually happens. A correct answer gets written carefully and fully qualified - "O(1) average, because a good hash spreads keys across buckets so each lookup touches only about one entry" - while wrong answers get written quickly and stay terse. Every author will drift this way, on every batch, without noticing. The #42 precedent applies: if the property is mechanical, check it mechanically rather than trusting a reviewer to count characters.

Note the authoring gate landed under #42 does not catch this at all, and correctly so - it grades each distractor in isolation for whether it encodes a real misconception. All 12 of these checks passed that bar. The defect is a property of the option **set**, which nothing currently inspects.

## What to build

A content-quality check that fails when a check's correct option is conspicuously longer than its distractors.

Design judgement to make and justify in the PR:

- **The threshold.** "Correct answer must never be longest" is too strict - sometimes it legitimately is, and a rule that cries wolf gets suppressed. Something proportional (correct option longer than roughly 1.3x the mean of the others, say) targets the systematic case while tolerating honest variation. Pick a number, state the reasoning, and make it easy to tune.
- **Where it runs.** `RealContentSmokeTest` already loads the real content directory and is skipped rather than failed when no content path is configured, so it is a natural home and it sits in a repo that has CI. Consider whether this belongs beside it or as its own test. It must **not** go in the loader: unlike #42's declared-misconception rule, a length imbalance is a quality smell rather than a corruption, and hard-failing content load over it would be wrong.
- **The message.** A failure must name the file, the correct option's length, the others' lengths, and what to do about it - the fix is to pad the distractors up to parity, not to truncate the correct answer into something inaccurate.

Also consider flagging the related tells while you are here, if they are cheap: the only grammatically-agreeing option, and the one option that is qualified ("often", "typically") among absolutes.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A check whose correct option is conspicuously longer than its distractors is flagged, naming the file and the measured lengths
- [ ] The threshold is proportional, documented, and tunable in one place
- [ ] Honest variation does not trip it - a check with roughly balanced options passes
- [ ] It is a quality check, not a load failure; malformed content still fails at load, this does not
- [ ] The content repo's `README.md` authoring section is updated so authors know the bar before they write, and knows this is enforced mechanically (separate PR in that repo - do not land cross-repo changes in one branch)
- [ ] `./test.sh` green

Both acceptance criteria are now met.

1. **Engine check** - the set-level answer-tell check landed in PR #62 alongside the serve-time option shuffling for #59.
2. **Authoring bar** - the option-parity section is in swe-prep-content's README.md ("Options must be at parity: no answer tells"), landed with the AI/ML pilot in swe-prep-content PR #4.

The pilot itself is the evidence this was worth doing: the correct answer was the longest option in 9 of 13 checks at one point, which is 69% exploitable by "pick the longest" with no knowledge of the material. Two things learned while fixing it, both recorded in the README:

- **A per-item threshold does not catch a set-level tell.** The per-item ratio check passed every item while the key was still the longest option in most of the set. The property that matters is the key's length *rank* across the whole batch.
- **Fixing a tell by inverting it just flips the signal.** Padding distractors made the key the *shortest* option. This recurred three times across different axes (length, hedging, specificity), so the authoring bar now calls for an explicit both-directions check.

issues.title: C14 - Working with AI coding agents (the practice, not the tooling)
issues.body:
## Parent

Part of the planning map: #1. Extends the topic catalog in firstmate `data/swe-topics-r8/report.md` section 1.4, Bucket C.

## What to build

Author **C14 - Working with AI coding agents** as a Bucket C practice concept.

The catalog already carries **B11 (LLM/AI tooling literacy)**, but B11 is deliberately pinned to *primitives*: what a token is, what a context window is, why models hallucinate, what an eval is. That is the API-level mental model.

This concept is the other half, and it is a **practice**, not a technology: how a working engineer actually collaborates with an AI coding agent on a real codebase. Companies are restructuring their engineering workflow around this right now, and it is increasingly asked about directly - "how do you use AI in your workflow" is becoming a standard question, and the weak answer ("I use it for boilerplate") is distinguishable from a strong one in the first sentence.

It belongs in Bucket C alongside code review etiquette (C3), PR workflow (C4), and version-control hygiene (C8), because it is the same category of thing: how work actually gets done on a team.

## Scope - the durable half

Follow B11's own discipline (see section 1.5 of the topics report): teach what will still be true in a year, not what is true this quarter.

**In scope (durable):**
- **Delegate vs write yourself.** What agents are reliably good at, what they are reliably bad at, and how to tell before you spend the time rather than after.
- **Review discipline for generated code.** Reviewing code you did not write, at volume, is a distinct skill from reviewing a colleague's PR - the failure mode is plausible-looking wrongness, not obvious wrongness. This is the single most load-bearing item in the concept.
- **Specification as the real input.** Why an under-specified request produces confidently wrong output, and why the skill transfers directly from writing a good ticket.
- **Verification over trust.** Tests, types, and executable checks as the thing that actually makes agent output safe - the arguments generalize past any tool.
- **Context management.** Why what the agent can see determines what it can do, and the practical consequences.
- **Where accountability sits.** You own the merged code. Interviewers probe this, and "the AI wrote it" is a disqualifying answer.
- **Honest limits.** Where this genuinely does not help, and why claiming otherwise reads as inexperience.

**Explicitly out of scope (volatile - it rots within a quarter and a stale confident claim is exactly the failure this pipeline exists to prevent):**
- Specific tool names, vendor feature lists, model names, pricing, capability comparisons.
- Prompt-phrasing tricks tied to a particular model's quirks.
- Benchmark numbers.

Tag `stability: VOLATILE` per issue #43's shelf-life split, and carry the refresh policy. **No answer key may depend on a fact that expires** - if a check can only be answered by knowing a current product's behaviour, it is the wrong check.

## Why this needs care

This is the hardest concept in the catalog to author honestly. The material is (a) genuinely new, so primary sources are thin and much of what is written about it is marketing or hype, and (b) contested, with credible engineers holding opposite positions on how much it helps. Both are conditions the protocol says to treat carefully.

Two consequences:
- **Source discipline is harder here, not easier.** Vendor blog posts are marketing, not primary sources. Prefer empirical studies, primary tool documentation for mechanism claims only, and practitioner accounts flagged as tier 3.
- **Where the honest answer is "the evidence is mixed", teach that.** A learner who can say "the research here is genuinely contested, and here is the shape of the disagreement" is *more* credible in an interview than one repeating a confident claim in either direction. Cut anything that cannot be defended; a thinner correct lesson beats a fuller one with a landmine.

Consider promoting this concept to **full rigor tier** despite being neither security nor concurrency: the operating rule says full tier applies to any concept "where the drafter or firstmate judges the fact surface contested", and this one plainly is.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] One lesson, 3-5 checks each carrying its own explanation, and a self-graded explain-in-your-own-words item
- [ ] Tagged `stability: VOLATILE` and carrying the refresh policy
- [ ] No check key depends on a current model, tool, vendor feature, price, or benchmark
- [ ] Contested claims are either taught as contested, with the disagreement named, or cut - never asserted as settled
- [ ] Rigor tier declared in the Claims Ledger, with the reasoning if it is promoted to full
- [ ] Nothing lands in the app repo; content lives only in the private content repo

issues.title: AnswerTellChecker misses the set-level connective-style tell (found 4/4 exploitable in production content)
issues.body:
## Parent

Part of the planning map: #1. Follows #59 and #60, which closed the position tell and the length tell.

## What to build

Extend `AnswerTellChecker` with a **set-level connective-style axis**: flag a check whose correct answer is the only option containing a causal connective (`since`, `because`, `as`, `so that`, and near neighbours), and equally flag the mirror case where the key is the only option *without* one.

## Why

This was found in production content by the red-team on swe-prep-content PR #5, and it is a clean, cheap, mechanical catch.

In all four newly authored checks of that batch, **every distractor carried a `since` clause and the key carried none**. "Pick the option that does not justify itself" scored 4 out of 4 with zero domain knowledge - a 100% exploit on that batch. For contrast, the previously merged 13 items hit the same pattern only once, so it is a regression an author can introduce without noticing rather than a standing property of the corpus.

Three properties make it worth automating rather than leaving to review:

1. **It survives option shuffling.** #59 randomised option order, which defeats position tells. This one is a property of the option *text*, so shuffling does nothing.
2. **The existing per-item length check cannot see it.** Same structural reason #60 existed: `AnswerTellChecker`'s 1.3x key-vs-distractor-mean ratio is a per-item length measure, and this tell is categorical and set-level.
3. **A careful human author following the documented bar still shipped it.** The drafter ran its own answer-tell self-check, cleared every axis the content repo's README names, and shipped this anyway. That is the signature of a check that belongs in code.

## The mirror-image trap - please build the check to catch both directions

This repo's dominant recurring failure is that **fixing a tell inverts it rather than removing it**: pad the distractors and the key becomes the shortest; soften the hedged distractors and the key becomes the only unhedged one. That pattern cost the AI/ML pilot four fix rounds.

So the check must fail **both** "key is the only option with a connective" and "key is the only option without one". The passing condition is that the key shares the property with at least one distractor - not that the property points a particular way.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A check whose key is the only option carrying a causal connective is flagged
- [ ] A check whose key is the only option lacking one is flagged, with equal severity
- [ ] A check whose key shares the property with at least one distractor passes
- [ ] The connective vocabulary is defined in one place and is easy to extend as new tells are found
- [ ] The existing four-item batch from swe-prep-content PR #5, in its pre-fix state, is caught by this check - use it as the regression fixture rather than a synthetic example
- [ ] The flag names the offending item and states which direction it failed, so an author can act without re-deriving

## Note for whoever picks this up

The corresponding authoring-side gap is being fixed separately in the content repo: its `README.md` option-parity section documents the length and lone-qualifier tells but never named connective style, while `CLAUDE.md` did. That doc fix and this engine check are complementary - the doc tells an author what to avoid, this check catches it when they miss.

issues.title: AnswerTellChecker's length axis is character-only and one-sided - word-count tell scored 41.2% in production content
issues.body:
## Parent

Part of the planning map: #1. Sibling of #65 (connective-style axis); follows #59 and #60.

## What to build

Extend `AnswerTellChecker`'s length axis to measure **word count as well as characters**, and to check **rank as well as ratio**, in both directions.

Four things, all of which the current check misses:

1. **Word count, not just characters.** The existing check is character-only.
2. **Rank, not just ratio.** A key can sit comfortably inside the 1.3x mean-ratio bar and still be the uniquely shortest or uniquely longest option. Flag the key being a unique extreme at either end.
3. **Two-sided ratio.** The current 1.3x bar only catches a key that is too *long*. A ratio of 0.57 is exactly as exploitable as 1.75 and is currently invisible.
4. **Do not reward a uniform-length template.** Collapsing every option to the same length is its own tell. If the check is ever used to drive automated repair, the guidance must be "key must not be a unique extreme", never "all options equal".

## Why - measured, not hypothetical

A corpus-wide audit on 2026-08-09 scored guessing strategies against the 25% four-option baseline:

- **"Pick the shortest answer by word count" scored 41.2%** on the AI/ML metrics corpus, and **36.0%** on the Core batch 1 corpus. Both were the single strongest exploit in their batch.
- On the same content, **character rank was already balanced** and the character ratio was inside the bar. The word tell hid entirely behind a passing character check.

Two production items showed how extreme this gets:

| item | key | distractors | word ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| `http-status-classes` | 13 words | 23, 24, 21 | 0.57 |
| `cache-no-cache-vs-no-store` | 16 words | 29, 24, 27 | 0.60 |

A learner who knows nothing picks the short option and is right both times.

Both shipped through a red-team, an adjudication pass, a re-gate, and an author's own self-check. The second of them shipped through a repair round that was *explicitly briefed on word-count parity* - the worker measured the ratio and never checked the rank. That is the signature of a check that belongs in code rather than in review.

## The mirror-image trap

Same warning as #65. This repo's dominant recurring failure is that fixing a tell inverts it rather than removing it. The passing condition is that the key is **not a unique extreme** - not that it points a particular way.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Word-count parity is measured alongside character parity
- [ ] A key that is the uniquely shortest option is flagged
- [ ] A key that is the uniquely longest option is flagged, with equal severity
- [ ] The ratio bar is two-sided: 1/1.3 is as much a failure as 1.3
- [ ] A key sitting mid-pack on both metrics passes, and items are not pushed toward uniform option length
- [ ] The pre-fix `http-status-classes` and `cache-no-cache-vs-no-store` items are the regression fixture, rather than synthetic examples - both are in swe-prep-content history
- [ ] The flag names the item, the metric, and the direction, so an author can act without re-deriving

## Note for whoever picks this up

#65 covers the connective-style axis and is being implemented separately. These are complementary and should not be merged into one change.

issues.title: Connective axis: 'as' produces mostly false alarms (3 of 4 flags on real content, at least 2 non-causal)
issues.body:
## Parent

Follow-up to #65, which shipped the connective-style axis in PR #68. Not a defect in that change - `as` is named explicitly in #65's own spec, so shipping it was correct. This issue is about the measured cost of keeping it.

## What was measured

Running #65's rule over the 29 four-option items on `swe-prep-content` `main` after PR #5 and PR #6 landed, one lexeme at a time, exactly as `connectiveStyle` does:

| lexeme | items it would flag |
|---|---|
| `since` | 0 |
| `because` | 1 |
| `as` | **3** |
| `so that` | 0 |

So `as` accounts for three of the four flags, and hand-inspection says **at least two of those three are false alarms** - the `as` is not causal:

- `aiml-metrics-specificity` - flagged ONLY-WITHOUT. All three distractors match on `as`, but the uses are `"another name for"` and `"wrongly flags **as** positive"`. Neither is a connective.
- `aiml-bv-high-bias` - flagged ONLY-WITH on a non-causal `as` in the key.

The one genuine catch in the set is `because`, on `aiml-bv-tradeoff`: all three distractors literally begin with "Because" and the key does not, which is a real "pick the one that doesn't justify itself" tell and exactly what #65 was built for.

## Why it matters

`AnswerTellChecker`'s own javadoc already states the principle - the grammatical-agreement axis was deliberately left out because "a shaky heuristic there would cry wolf". `as` is the most polysemous word in the list (`the same as`, `such as`, `flags as positive`, `as a result`), and a checker whose majority of flags are false trains an author to skim past all of them, including the true ones.

## Options

1. **Drop `as` from `CONNECTIVES`.** Cheapest. Costs the ability to catch a genuine lone-`as` causal tell, which was never observed in the corpus.
2. **Require a causal context for `as`** - e.g. only count sentence-initial `As ` or `, as ` - keeping the catch while dropping `flags as positive` and `another name for`. More code, needs its own fixture.
3. **Keep it and accept the noise**, but rank or tag findings so a low-confidence lexeme reads differently from a high-confidence one.

Recommendation: option 2 if it stays cheap, option 1 otherwise. Either way, keep the measurement above as the regression fixture, since it is real corpus data rather than synthetic.

## Note

Findings are advisory and do not gate anything, so this is a signal-quality issue, not a correctness one. It does not need to be urgent.

issues.title: C14 teaches an uncited human-vs-generated review signal as a settled difference
issues.body:
## Finding

`agentic-coding-practice.json` and check `agents-review-discipline` teach that human mistakes usually leave surface traces while generated mistakes usually do not, and make that comparison the key to a scored item. The C14 claims ledger itself concedes that this is a framing, not a measured finding.

## Evidence

The cited Perry et al. study measures security outcomes and participants' confidence, not code reviewers or comparative surface traces: https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.03622

The cited package-hallucination study establishes that nonexistent imports occur and can recur; it does not compare how visible human and generated defects are to reviewers: https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.10279

No cited source supports the universal comparative words “human mistakes usually” and “generated mistakes usually”. Because `agents-review-discipline` turns that unsupported comparison into the correct answer, this is more than optional lesson color.

## Decision needed

Choose one: (1) source a reviewer study that supports the comparative claim; (2) relabel it in learner-facing prose and the check as a practitioner heuristic with explicit uncertainty; or (3) replace the scored item with the independently supportable rule to review against requirements, contracts, and error paths regardless of authorship. This pass did not make that product/framing decision.

issues.title: C14 delegation-by-verification-cost rule is useful framing, not an evidenced finding
issues.body:
## Finding

`agentic-coding-practice.json` and `agentic-coding-explain.json` teach “decide what to delegate by the cost of checking, not by the size of the job.” The ledger correctly labels this as framing, but the learner-facing lesson presents it as the durable decision rule.

## Evidence tension

The cited controlled GitHub Copilot experiment used a self-contained HTTP-server task with a relatively cheap oracle: https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.06590

The much larger field experiments report uplift on ordinary enterprise work, where correctness is not shown to be cheap to verify: https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/10.1287/mnsc.2025.00535

Those studies do not establish verification cost as the moderator that explains delegation value. The current lesson now admits that evidence does not line up behind the framing, but still elevates it as the primary rule.

## Decision needed

Either keep it explicitly as an interview/practice heuristic, commission evidence for it, or narrow it to the noncontroversial claim that tasks with independent, fast failure signals are easier to verify. This pass left the choice out of the content PR because it is a curriculum-framing decision, not an unambiguous factual correction.
